demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is 52, South Asian, divorced, and works as a maid, moving quietly through other people’s homes with a practiced attention to detail that has become part of how he survives. He speaks about himself with restraint, often pausing before answering, as though he is checking first whether his words might cause harm. That carefulness seems to have deepened since the day his life changed.

The accident happens at work. He is carrying out one of his usual tasks, focused on finishing quickly and correctly, when a moment of distraction turns catastrophic. He describes it in fragments rather than a full story, and even those fragments come with a visible tightening around his mouth. Something slips, someone is injured, and in an instant he goes from routine labor to horror. He had not meant for anything to happen. That fact matters to him almost painfully. He returns to it over and over: that he was trying to work, that he was not careless, that he never imagined his hands could be connected to such serious injury. Yet the memory does not allow him the comfort of innocence. He carries the scene with him as if he is still standing in it, frozen, hearing the sounds, seeing the aftermath, and knowing that life for another person has been altered because of him.

In the days after the accident, he does not feel like himself. He becomes jumpy at sudden noises, and he startles more than he used to when a door shuts hard or a voice rises unexpectedly. He sleeps poorly. Even when he falls asleep, the night does not feel like rest. He wakes already tense, often with his heart racing, and then lies in bed replaying the event in pieces, trying to locate the exact second when things went wrong. He wants to find a point where he could have stopped it, as though punishment might be avoided if he can identify his failure precisely enough.

At work, he begins to move differently. He slows down, checks and rechecks tasks, and avoids anything that feels even slightly risky. The care that once made him a reliable worker becomes strained by fear. He notices himself hesitating before lifting or carrying things, and his body reacts before his mind catches up. His shoulders tighten. His breathing shortens. He becomes preoccupied with the possibility that a small mistake will become another disaster. Because of this, work is no longer simply work; it is a test he fears failing every hour.

He also withdraws from people. He is divorced and lives with a long-standing sense that his life has narrowed over time, but after the accident that narrowing becomes more severe. He keeps conversations brief. He avoids talking about the incident with family or coworkers because the shame is immediate and overwhelming. He worries that if he explains what happened, others will hear not an accident but a moral failure. He imagines judgment before it is spoken. At times he can feel himself pulling away even while sitting in the same room, his mind elsewhere, occupied by the memory and by the question of what kind of man he is now.

Certain reminders set off waves of distress. If he sees someone injured, hears sirens, or notices a workplace hazard, the accident returns with force. He may feel suddenly hot, nauseated, and unable to think clearly. In those moments he feels as though the present disappears and he is back in the original scene, helpless and overwhelmed. Afterward he is exhausted, ashamed of how shaken he becomes, and angry at himself for not having “moved on.” Yet moving on feels impossible when guilt has become woven into his daily life.

Over time, he begins to see himself through the accident. He speaks less about his plans and more about what he has lost: his ease, his confidence, his ability to trust his own hands. He continues to work because he must, but he does so under a constant cloud of dread. On the surface he remains composed and functional, the kind of man who finishes the job and leaves quietly. Inside, he is still living in the aftermath, trying to carry a memory he cannot set down.
